intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene (179605) on chromosome 6p21.1. Digenic retinitis pigmentosa is caused by double heterozygosity for mutations in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene (180721).

checks.claim: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
checks.explanation: RDS is an alias of PRPH2, and autosomal dominant inheritance implies heterozygous mutations. However, the abstract does not name the RP7 designation or say the mutations are heterozygous. It says only that some cases of ADRP are due to RDS mutations.

checks.claim: The PRPH2 gene is located on chromosome 6p21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p, showing tight linkage with the gene for peripherin
checks.explanation: The paper places the peripherin gene on 6p. The finer band 6p21.1 is standard OMIM cytogenetic nomenclature that restates the paper's location, so it counts as supported.

checks.claim: Digenic retinitis pigmentosa is caused by double heterozygosity for mutations in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The abstract says that in these families only people who are double heterozygous for PRPH2 (peripherin/RDS) and ROM1 mutations develop RP, which it calls digenic RP.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 is a form of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa caused by mutation in the gene encoding peripherin-RDS, a photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein. The phenotype is variable: the same mutation can cause retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy, or fundus flavimaculatus within one family, and pericentral RP, macular dystrophy, and widespread RP have been seen in members of the same family. A digenic form occurs in individuals who are double heterozygotes for mutations in peripherin/RDS and ROM1.

checks.explanation: Describes the 6p peripherin-linked form as autosomal dominant RP.

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) described a family in which a 75-year-old woman, her 2 daughters (aged 44 and 50 years), and her 49-year-old son carried the same peripherin/RDS deletion but had different phenotypes. The mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa that progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years; at age 44 years her ERG was moderately abnormal, but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. The other daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus; her peripheral visual field was preserved, but her ERG was moderately abnormal. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years, with pericentral scotomas, a markedly abnormal ERG, and punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects on fluorescein angiography.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) characterized French families with PRPH2-associated autosomal dominant RP. The disease was of moderate severity: 78% of eyes had visual acuity of 1-0.5, and 52% retained more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. Phenotypes were highly variable; in some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy was found in some members while widespread RP was present in others. The authors suggested that mild cases could be underdiagnosed.

paragraphs.text: Farrar et al. (1991) typed members of an Irish pedigree with late-onset autosomal dominant RP with a series of chromosome 6p markers and mapped the disease locus to 6p. Two-point lod scores were positive with several markers, including D6S105 (Z = 6.081 at theta = 0.00) and RDS (Z = 5.376 at theta = 0.00). Multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 6.6 at HLA-DRA. The authors concluded that the data provided direct evidence for an additional autosomal dominant RP locus and strongly implicated peripherin-rds, the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, as a candidate gene.

A stop codon at codon 258 was found in a family with adult vitelliform macular dystrophy. The authors suggested that certain amino acids in peripherin-RDS may have different functional significance in cones and rods.
